title: Welfare assessment in a colony rabbit run
subtitle: A colony run that looks busy is not automatically a happy one. Read the social dynamics before you close the gate.
excerpt: Colony housing lets rabbits express natural social behaviour: foraging together, resting in contact, using tunnels and hides. It also concentrates hierarchical aggression in a way a single hutch does not. Reading body language and resource competition early stops minor bullying from becoming injury.
sourceNotes: RSPCA rabbit welfare assessment notes. British Rabbit Council colony housing guidance. Anne McBride, Why Does My Rabbit...? (2001), chapters on social behaviour. RWAF (Rabbit Welfare Association and Fund) species-specific housing standards.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rabbit chewing or pulling out fur from another rabbit, or from itself. A stress behaviour. Patchy fur loss concentrated on the flanks, face, or back indicates a rabbit being barbered.
The highest-ranking rabbit in a group. Determines who eats first, who uses a preferred rest spot, and who mounts others regardless of sex or neutering status.

content.text: A colony run with tunnels, hides, and space for foraging meets a rabbit's environmental needs in a way a hutch cannot. The challenge is that it also allows the
dominant rabbit
to control resources and push lower-ranked animals away from food, water, and shelter. A welfare assessment is a five-minute structured observation, not a glance through the gate.
What to assess at each daily check
All rabbits visible and accounted for.
All rabbits eating. A rabbit pushed off the feeder repeatedly and not eating is being excluded.
No rabbit sitting hunched in a corner or pressed into a hide during active feeding time. A hunched posture with eyes half-closed is a pain or fear signal.
Coat condition across all animals. Look for
barbering
, patchy fur loss on the face, neck, or flanks of one rabbit indicates another is pulling its fur.
Bite wounds. Small rabbits and juveniles are most vulnerable. Part the fur on the neck and flanks of any rabbit that sits apart from the group.
Reading dominance interactions
Normal social behaviour in a bonded group includes mutual grooming, resting in contact, chasing during bonding, and chin-marking on shared objects. These are not problems.
Signs that dominance has tipped into bullying:
One rabbit repeatedly chases another away from food or water with no break in the pattern.
Mounting that continues despite the mounted rabbit clearly trying to escape.
Bite wounds found on the same animal repeatedly.
A rabbit losing weight while others in the group maintain condition.
Interventions when bullying is confirmed

Add resource duplication: a second hay station, second water bottle, and second food bowl placed at opposite ends of the run. Most feeding-related aggression is a competition problem, not a personality one.
Add more hides. Rabbits need visual barriers between them when they want to disengage. An empty run with no hides forces subordinate animals into sight of the dominant rabbit constantly.
If bullying continues after adjusting the environment, separate the bully or the victim temporarily. Then reassess the group.

Neutered pairs or small groups of three to five work well. Entire bucks with multiple does produces fighting between bucks and constant breeding. Entire does in a group sometimes fight. The most stable colony is neutered same-sex pairs or small neutered mixed groups, with introductions done carefully on neutral territory before releasing into the main run.
